what: Prints the effective username of the current session.
why: First question in any host triage: which identity is this shell running as. Confirms whether an attacker landed as a service account or a privileged user.
useCase: Checking the context of a suspicious reverse shell captured in an EDR process tree.

what: Shows user id, primary group and all supplementary groups.
why: Group membership is where privilege actually lives. An account in sudo, docker, lxd or adm has an escalation path even if it looks unprivileged.
useCase: Confirming whether a compromised service account could escalate to root.

what: Lists network interfaces and their addresses.
why: Establishes which address the host actually owns, so firewall and proxy logs can be attributed to it correctly through NAT.
useCase: Mapping an internal alert source address to the right host during triage.

what: Displays sockets: listening services and established connections.
why: Shows live command-and-control channels and unexpected listeners with the owning process, which is the fastest confirmation of an active implant.
useCase: Confirming a beaconing host still holds an open session to an external address.

what: Lists running processes with their parents, users and arguments.
why: Parentage and command line are the core of execution analysis. A shell whose parent is a web server process is an immediate finding.
useCase: Finding a suspicious child process under a legitimate daemon.

what: Live view of processes ordered by resource usage.
why: Cryptominers, encryption routines and bulk staging show as sustained CPU or IO from an unexpected user.
useCase: Triage of a host reported as slow after an alert for unauthorised software.

what: Legacy socket and routing table listing, still present on older estates.
why: Same value as ss on hosts where ss is unavailable, and often what an attacker's own commands show in shell history.
useCase: Reviewing connections on a legacy appliance with no modern tooling.

what: Searches text for a pattern.
why: The single most used log-analysis command. Pulls every occurrence of an account, address or indicator out of gigabytes of text.
useCase: Extracting every authentication failure for one account across a month of logs.

what: Prints a file to standard output.
why: Reads small configuration and evidence files intact - crontabs, unit files, authorized_keys - without a pager altering what you see.
useCase: Inspecting a suspected persistence entry found by an EDR alert.

what: Pages through a file interactively with search.
why: Safe way to read very large logs without loading them into memory, with in-file search for indicators.
useCase: Reading a multi-gigabyte log during an investigation on a live host.

what: Shows the end of a file, optionally following new lines.
why: Most incidents are recent. The last lines of a log are where an active intrusion is visible first.
useCase: Watching authentication logs while a suspected brute force is in progress.

what: Shows the beginning of a file.
why: Used to sample a log's format and confirm timestamp conventions before writing parsing or grep patterns.
useCase: Checking whether an exported log is in UTC before building a timeline.

what: Searches the filesystem by name, time, size, owner or permissions.
why: Locates attacker-dropped files by modification window, and finds world-writable or SUID binaries used for escalation.
useCase: Listing every file written on a host within the suspected intrusion window.

what: Queries the systemd journal.
why: On modern Linux the authoritative record of service starts, failures and authentication lives here rather than in flat files.
useCase: Proving when a malicious systemd service was first started.

what: Lists and inspects systemd units.
why: Rogue services are a common Linux persistence mechanism; this shows what is enabled to start at boot and where its unit file lives.
useCase: Enumerating persistence after confirming a Linux host was compromised.

what: Shows historical login sessions from wtmp.
why: Gives a session-level view of who logged in, from where and for how long, complementing per-event auth logs.
useCase: Confirming interactive access following a successful password guess.

what: Lists scheduled jobs for a user.
why: Cron is the oldest and still most common Linux persistence location, including per-user crontabs that host-level scans miss.
useCase: Checking every account for scheduled callbacks after an intrusion.

what: Prints the current user, and with flags the full token privileges and groups.
why: Privilege enumeration in one command. SeDebugPrivilege or SeBackupPrivilege on an ordinary account is an escalation path.
useCase: Assessing what a compromised session could reach before containment.

what: Displays network configuration, and manages the DNS resolver cache.
why: The DNS cache can still hold recently resolved malicious domains after the process that resolved them has exited.
useCase: Recovering command-and-control domains from a host with no local DNS logging.

what: Lists connections and listening ports with owning process ids.
why: Ties an external connection to a specific process, turning a network alert into a host finding.
useCase: Identifying which process is maintaining a beacon to an external address.

what: Lists running processes, optionally with services and modules.
why: Rapid triage of a suspicious host, including which service is hosted inside a shared svchost instance.
useCase: Checking for unexpected processes running as SYSTEM.

what: Reports build, patch level, domain and uptime.
why: Patch level explains which vulnerabilities were reachable, and uptime bounds how far back volatile evidence can go.
useCase: Establishing whether a host was missing the patch for an exploited vulnerability.

what: Queries, exports and manages Windows event logs.
why: Pulls the exact security events needed for a timeline off a host, and shows whether a log was cleared or resized to destroy evidence.
useCase: Exporting logon events for the intrusion window from a suspect server.

what: Lists interactive and remote desktop sessions on the host.
why: Shows live attacker sessions, including disconnected sessions that remain active and are easily missed.
useCase: Confirming an adversary is still logged in before isolating a server.

what: Views and manages users, groups, shares and sessions.
why: Adversaries use it for discovery and for adding accounts to privileged groups; defenders use it to check what changed.
useCase: Verifying whether a compromised account was added to a privileged group.

what: Lists and inspects scheduled tasks.
why: Scheduled tasks are the most common Windows persistence mechanism, and the task action reveals the payload path.
useCase: Enumerating persistence after a confirmed endpoint compromise.

what: Reads registry keys and values.
why: Run keys, services and policy values are where persistence and defence-evasion changes are recorded.
useCase: Checking autorun locations on a host flagged for a suspicious binary.

what: Queries and inspects Windows services.
why: Service binary paths are a classic persistence and escalation target; an unquoted or user-writable path is a finding.
useCase: Confirming a service binary was replaced with an attacker payload.

what: PowerShell cmdlet for querying event logs with filters.
why: Far more capable than wevtutil for building timelines: filter by id, time range and provider, then output structured objects.
useCase: Correlating failed and successful logons across a suspected brute-force window.

what: Resolves a hostname or address using DNS.
why: Confirms what a suspicious domain currently resolves to, and whether it points at infrastructure already seen in the investigation.
useCase: Checking whether two suspicious domains share hosting infrastructure.

what: Detailed DNS query tool showing full response sections.
why: Reveals record type, TTL and authority - a very low TTL on a newly registered domain is a strong tunnelling or fast-flux indicator.
useCase: Investigating a domain suspected of carrying data in TXT records.

what: Queries registration data for a domain or address block.
why: Registration age and registrar are triage signals; a domain registered days before the alert is materially more suspicious.
useCase: Establishing that a phishing domain was registered two days before the campaign.

what: Captures and displays packets from an interface.
why: Ground truth when logs are ambiguous. Confirms the actual destination, protocol and volume of a suspected channel.
useCase: Capturing evidence of an active beacon before containment.

what: Filter syntax for examining captured traffic in Wireshark.
why: Isolates the few relevant conversations from a capture containing millions of packets.
useCase: Extracting the server name indication values from a suspected C2 session.

what: Scans hosts for open ports and service versions.
why: Used by defenders to verify exposure of a service after an incident, and recognised in logs as the shape of adversary discovery.
useCase: Confirming whether a management port was genuinely reachable from a network segment. Authorised internal use only.

what: Transfers data to or from a URL and shows headers.
why: Safely inspects response headers and status of a suspicious host from an isolated analysis system without rendering content.
useCase: Checking a phishing site's redirect chain from a sandboxed analyst VM.

what: Shows the network path taken to a destination.
why: Distinguishes a genuinely external destination from one that is internally routed, which changes how an egress alert is interpreted.
useCase: Verifying that traffic left the corporate perimeter rather than staying internal.

what: Submitting a file hash to a reputation or intelligence platform.
why: Establishes whether a binary is known malicious, known good, or unseen. An unseen hash on one host is more concerning than a widely known one.
example: sha256sum suspicious.exe   then search the resulting hash
useCase: Triaging a binary an EDR flagged on a single endpoint. Never upload the file itself if it may contain company data.

what: Checking an address against intelligence sources and passive DNS.
why: Shows prior malicious use, hosting provider and shared infrastructure - and whether blocking it would break a legitimate service.
example: Look up 91.203.5.12: ASN, geolocation, passive DNS, prior reports
useCase: Deciding whether an outbound destination justifies a perimeter block.

what: Finding other domains and addresses historically linked to an indicator.
why: Turns one confirmed indicator into the full infrastructure set, which is how the true blast radius of a campaign is found.
example: Pivot cdn-sync-delivery.net to its historical addresses, then to other domains on those addresses
useCase: Discovering additional internal hosts that contacted related infrastructure but never alerted.

what: Reading Received chains, authentication results and envelope fields.
why: Reveals the true sending path and whether SPF, DKIM and DMARC actually passed, separating spoofing from a compromised legitimate sender.
useCase: Determining whether a payment-change request came from a genuinely compromised supplier mailbox.

what: Rewriting indicators so they cannot be accidentally clicked or auto-resolved.
why: Prevents accidental navigation and prevents security tooling from silently resolving attacker infrastructure when a report is shared.
useCase: Writing indicators into an incident report or ticket.

what: Ordering evidence from all sources into one UTC sequence.
why: An intrusion only becomes comprehensible in order. The timeline exposes the gap between first activity and detection, which is usually the report's key number.
example: One row per event: UTC time, host, user, action, source of evidence
useCase: Building the attack timeline section of an incident report.

what: Determining every account, host and dataset the adversary could have reached.
why: Containment that covers only observed activity leaves the adversary the access you did not look for.
example: For each compromised credential: where else did it authenticate, what did it have rights to
useCase: Scoping a coordinated credential reset before it is executed.

what: Assigning observed behaviour to tactics and techniques.
why: Creates a shared vocabulary for the report and exposes which stages had no detection coverage.
example: T1566.002 phishing link, T1078 valid accounts, T1053.005 scheduled task, T1021.002 SMB admin shares
useCase: Producing the technique mapping section of an investigation report.
